# Notes on 2 Corinthians 4

**Coverage:** My research tools ran out before I could read sources on verses 11, 12, 15 and 16, so those verses are missing or thin below. I found nothing on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so that section is left out. The Catholic/Orthodox material is all from Chrysostom.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Paul preached boldly. Thinking about how great his calling was gave him courage to face his troubles. The Greek word for "lose heart" suggests a fainthearted coward. Paul also preached humbly, because he knew he had his calling by mercy, not by his own works. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- Ellicott: "this ministry" is the ministry of the new covenant described in chapter 3. "Received mercy" shows Paul knew he was unworthy of it. Being called to such a work made him strong, so he could not give way to cowardice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the Greek word for "deceitfully" appears only here in the New Testament and means "to dilute or adulterate." Paul preached neither a hidden gospel nor a watered-down one. Guzik quotes Spurgeon against preachers who adjust truth to suit the age. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- Ellicott: opponents had accused Paul of "craftiness" (compare 12:16). He appealed not to people's tastes but to their conscience, knowing he spoke before God, who judges hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: if people reject the gospel, the fault is not Paul's or the gospel's. He quotes Calvin's picture: the sun is no less bright because the blind cannot see it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- Ellicott: "those who are perishing" are not only Judaizing teachers. They are everyone now on the road to ruin. The present tense leaves room for them to change. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm

**v. 4**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the translation "god of this age." It quotes Bengel calling this "a great and horrible description of the devil." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-4.htm
- Barnes says Satan is called "god" not because he has any divine attributes, but because he actually has the homage of the people of this world as their god. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-4.htm (text read on the fetched page)
- Guzik says unbelievers are not innocent victims: people love the darkness (John 3:19), and Satan works to keep them in it. He also stresses that Satan can only blind those who do not believe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- GotQuestions says God sets limits on Satan, and his domain is limited to unbelievers. https://www.gotquestions.org/Satan-god-world.html
- Ellicott: the word for "light" is a special form meaning radiance. Christ as "image of God" echoes Genesis 1:26. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Paul did not put himself at the centre of his preaching. He quotes Hodge: preaching that only aims at moral improvement is like trying to grow fruit without trees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- Ellicott: Paul is answering a charge that his preaching was self-centred. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm
- Matthew Henry: Ministers are servants to the souls of men; they must avoid becoming servants to the humours or the lusts of men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-7.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: this verse is the deliberate opposite of v. 4. The god of this world blinds, while the true God calls light out of darkness, as in Genesis 1:3. "Shone" points to the moment of conversion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm
- Guzik: this describes Paul's own conversion on the Damascus road (Acts 9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/
- Matthew Henry: As light was the first-born of the first creation, so it is in the new creation: the illumination of the Spirit is his first work upon the soul. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_004.cfm

**v. 7**
- What is the treasure? Pulpit says it is the "light" of verses 4–6. It suggests the image comes from Gideon's torches hidden in clay jars (Judges 7). https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/4-7.htm
- Gill says the treasure is the gospel itself, for not grace, nor Christ, but the Gospel is here meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-7.htm
- Ellicott: Eastern kings stored gold in clay jars. The phrase may also answer taunts about Paul's physical weakness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm
- Calvin: a treasure is not worth less because the jar holding it is cheap. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-7.html
- MacArthur: God delights in such clay pots because it leaves no question about the source of power. https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-28/priceless-treasure-in-clay-pots-part-2

**vv. 8–9**
- Ellicott: each pair has a military background, like a soldier pursued but not abandoned, or struck down but not killed. One translation he cites renders "perplexed, but not in despair" as "bewildered, but not benighted." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm
- Barclay's paraphrase ends: We are knocked down, but not knocked out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-7.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the word for "dying" literally means "deadness," the state of a corpse. It pictures a man whose life was one long fight with illness and who was "dying daily." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/4.htm
- Utley (bible.org) links this to Paul's physical scars (Galatians 6:17): As our earthly vessel is broken, the treasure inside is more visible. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-4

**v. 12**
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the Corinthians owe their spiritual life to Paul's preaching. That is how v. 12 connects to v. 13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm

**v. 13**
- The quotation is Psalm 116:10, taken from the Greek Old Testament (LXX). Pulpit says this psalm fitted Paul's mood because it was written in trouble sustained by faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
- Ellicott suggests the psalm comforted Paul in his daily struggle with illness. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
- Bengel: Faith produced in the soul immediately speaks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm

**v. 14**
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): the same Spirit who raised Christ will raise believers and present them together with the Corinthians. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-13.html

**v. 17**
- Poole: the troubles are called light only compared with the weight of glory, and momentary only compared with eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-17.htm
- The Geneva notes add that troubles are called light because they pass away quickly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-17.htm
- Barnes suggests "weight" may picture a robe or crown heavy with gold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Chrysostom, as cited by JFB: we are not to fix our minds on visible things, whether trouble or comfort, so we are neither drawn away by comfort nor scared off by trouble. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Cr/2Cr_004.cfm

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 13: what is "the spirit of faith"?** This is the clearest disagreement I found.
- **Reformed (Calvin):** "spirit of faith" is a figure of speech for faith itself, because it is a gift of the Holy Spirit. His editor notes that Calvin also used this verse in the *Institutes* as proof that the Spirit plants faith in us. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom40.x.iii.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** the Holy Spirit causes faith, which is why he is called the "Spirit of faith". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
- **Presbyterian (Barnes):** the phrase means substantially the same as faith itself; a believing sense or impression of the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-13.html
- **Methodist (Wesley):** it is the spirit that animated the saints of old; David, in particular. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-13.html
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** it is not definitely the Holy Spirit, but the human spirit in fellowship with the Divine. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
- **Meyer** (a Lutheran scholar, though I didn't confirm that from the page): it is the same Holy Spirit working faith, not: the believing frame of mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
- **Two middle and modern positions:**
  - Vincent says it blends both meanings: faith as a gift of the Spirit of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-13.htm
  - Kruse, quoted by Precept Austin, prefers the human-attitude reading. Paul is not making a point about the Holy Spirit being the one who inspires faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-4-commentary
  - A Reformed Baptist writer on Monergism says the choice is of small consequence to us now. https://www.monergism.com/spirit-faith

**v. 4: who is "the god of this age"?** Almost everyone says Satan, but Barnes reports that some Church Fathers took it as the true God, and that Methodist Adam Clarke inclines to this opinion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-4.htm

**v. 4: how to respond in practice.** Guzik (Calvary Chapel; enduringword is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list) draws a prayer lesson: We should ask God to shine His light, to bind the blinding work of Satan, and to give faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/

**v. 17: does suffering cause the glory?** Piper (Baptist, Desiring God) stresses the verb. The text doesn't say glory merely *follows* suffering; it says suffering is *preparing* it, so that "Every millisecond of your misery is producing a glory you will get because of that suffering." https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-glory-of-god-in-the-sight-of-eternity/excerpts/none-of-our-misery-is-meaningless

---

## 3. Other views

**Church Fathers on v. 4.** Pulpit says some early Fathers, fighting the Manichaean idea of two gods, read the verse as "God hath blinded the understandings of the unbelievers of this world." It says they did so in defiance of the plain meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/4-4.htm
- Guzik names Augustine, Origen and Chrysostom among them. He agrees with Calvin that they were more eager to defeat opponents than to explain Paul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-4/

**Chrysostom (Orthodox and Catholic Father, read on newadvent.org):**
- **v. 7:** he presents it as proof of God's power that an earthen vessel could bear such splendor and keep such a treasure. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Cr/2Cr_004.cfm
- **v. 7, in a sermon on Eutropius:** he links the clay vessel to baptism. In baptism, he says, his nature is remade and the fire of the Spirit recasts it, and it is turned into a harder ware. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1915.htm
- **vv. 8–9:** a vessel even of adamant could not carry such a treasure, yet the clay vessel bears it unharmed through God's grace. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220209.htm
- **v. 18:** Paul says "things seen," not just "afflictions," to cover both punishment and rest, so that we should be neither puffed up by the one nor overborne by the other. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220209.htm

**A Christadelphian reading of v. 4** (outside mainstream Christianity): "the god of this world" was the ruler of the Jewish age, not Satan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-4.html

**A note on v. 7 from the Restoration Movement** (Gann): the "surpassing power" includes the apostles' miracles of healing the sick, casting out devils. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/4-7.html
